newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Telecommunications deregulation a trend in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Telecommunications deregulation a trend in Asia.

text.p: Singapore joins the push to deregulate Asia's telecommunications markets on April 1 when its largest telecoms provider, Singapore Telecommunications Ltd, relinquishes its once-prized monopoly of the domestic market.
SingTel, as it is commonly known, has had the monopoly on telecommunications services since it was privatised in 1992.
Come April 1, MobileOne will become a competitor in the mobile phone market, while three other companies will launch rival pager services.
In other parts of Asia the heat is on to break up old monopolies and, in some places, sooner rather than later.
JAPAN

The push toward deregulation is particularly evident in Japan. The country's main domestic operator Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp will form a holding company and be split into three companies under a bill to be passed by Japan's Diet, or parliament, by the end of June.
NTT looks to begin the process as soon as possible and already is looking to enter international services later this year, among other things.
HONG KONG
Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd is still the dominant telecoms operator in the territory, but deregulation and competition are eating into its position.
The government ended the company's monopoly on domestic fixed-line services in 1995.

Hongkong Telecom still has a monopoly on international voice traffic, but the government is holding talks on the subject with the company and analysts expect the monopoly will not last until its designated ending in 2006.

The result of the talks will affect Hong Kong's international position, especially within the context of the World Trade Organisation, and its domestic situation in which local calls are essentially free.
TAIWAN
Taiwan in January awarded eight mobile phone franchises to local consortiums, most of which were paired with global telecom giants.
However, Taiwan restricts foreign ownership of any telecoms venture at 20 percent to guard against a foreign monopoly.
The government has said that the dismantling of the island's telecoms company is a key liberalisation aimed at ensuring Taiwan's entry to the World Trade Organisation.
Analysts expect the local telecoms market, long monopolised by the state, to double in size in three to five years.
MALAYSIA
Currently there are five operators with fixed national and international gateway licences, and a total of six operators of mobile cellular services in the country.
But analysts say there is room for more change.
Tariffs are still subject to a price ceiling, with operators able to offer special discounts, but not indefinitely.
Such changes were seen more likely to occur after 1999, when Malaysia will allow consumers equal access to all the fixed-line operators in the country.
Foreign companies are allowed to own up to 30 percent of Malaysian companies.
Analysts said it was unlikely that large foreign operators would be allowed to provide services in direct competition with local players in the foreseeable future.
THE PHILIPPINES

The Philippines telecommunications sector was liberalised in 1993 with the passage of two laws that divided the country into service areas and required interconnection among local players assigned in the 11 areas of the country.
Prior to these laws, the Philippine Long Distance Telecommunications Co dominated the market.
The country now has 11 international gateway facility operators, 12 paging operators, five cellular phone companies and 11 local exchange operators.
Analysts see consolidation and mergers as the future trend to help the overcrowded sector achieve economies of scale.
"We think only four to five telecom firms will remain," Helen Alvarez, research director at All Asia Securities said.
Philippine telecoms firms are also aware of the need to "re-balance" rates to lessen dependence on revenues from international calls.
